source_text: παρθένον, οὐκ ἦν καὶ ἐν οὐρανῷ τῇ οὐσίᾳ, ὡς τῇ διανοίᾳ, ἀλλὰ τότε ἐπὶ γῆς διέτριβεν μόνον. οὐδὲ τοῖς αἰῶσίν εἰσιν ἀπερίληπτοι· «ὁ ποιῶν» γάρ, φησί, «τοὺς ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ πνεύματα, καὶ τοὺς λειτουργοὺς αὐτοῦ πῦρ φλέγον.» 4.7 οὐχ ἕν τι τῶν γινομένων παρὰ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος ποιοῦσιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ λειτουργοῦσιν αὐτῷ, ὡς ἔδειξεν ὁ ἀρχάγγελος Γαβριήλ, διακονησάμενος πρὸς τὴν θεοτόκον Μαρίαν καὶ εἰπών· «πνεῦμα ἅγιον ἐλεύσεται ἐπὶ σέ.» οὔτε οὖν ναὸς αὐτῶν ἐστιν ὁ ἄνθρωπος, καθά ἐστιν τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τοῦ πνεύματος αὐτοῦ καὶ τοῦ μονογενοῦς υἱοῦ. οὐ συμπεριλαμβάνονται μετὰ τοῦ θεοῦ. οὐ μία τίς ἐστιν ὑπόστασις ἀγγελική, ἀλλὰ καὶ δυσαρίθμητος. 4.8 τὸ δὲ ὑπερπάμφαες ἅγιον πνεῦμα συμφυῶς καὶ ἑνοειδῶς ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρρήτου καὶ ὑπερουσίου καὶ προουσίου καὶ καθολικῆς καὶ ἀμόρφου προῆλθεν ἀχρόνως πατρικῆς ὑποστάσεως, καὶ προσηγόρευται θεῖον· ἕν τέ ἐστιν ἀπλήθυντον, ἀγαθόν, ἄφθονον, ἀπρόσιτον, ἀπερίγραφον πάσαις νοήσεσιν, ἀπειροδύναμον, ἀνέκλεκτον, μόνως ὑπάρχον· καὶ φύσει ἅγιόν τε καὶ πνεῦμα τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ οὐδὲν ὂν τῶν πάντων, ἀλλὰ θεὸς ἐν οὐρανῷ τε ὢν καὶ συνὼν ἡμῖν, αἴτιος πᾶσιν πάντων καλῶν· παρὼν μὲν τοῖς ὅλοις ἀύλως, ἀνειδέως, ἀμετασχηματίστως· 4.9 οὐκ ἐξιστάμενος δὲ τοῦ συνιδρῦσθαι ἀφράστως τῷ πατρί, καὶ ἐξαπλούμενος πάντη καὶ χωρῶν, καὶ ἐν ἅπασιν ἀμιγῶς κατοικῶν· καὶ ταῖς ἐννοίαις ἡμῶν τε καὶ τῶν ἡμῖν ἀοράτων ἐμβατεύων, καὶ ἀκριβῶν ἅπαντα, καίτοι πάντα εἰδώς· καὶ ἀφώνως ἐνηχῶν, καὶ ψυχῶν ἐπακούων ἔνδοθεν σιγῇ κραζουσῶν, καὶ πάσας ἐπὶ πᾶσιν οἰκτείρων ἀμελλητί, καὶ ἐπιρωννύων, καὶ εὐφροσύνην ἄφατον ταῖς ἑκασταχοῦ φύσεσιν ἐνδιδούς· περιέχων τοῦδε τοῦ παντὸς τὴν σύστασιν, καὶ πάντα ἔχων ὑφ' ἑαυτῷ· καὶ θεσπεσίῳ φωτίζων φωτὶ καὶ εὐεργετῶν τῇ ἀπλέτῳ αὐτοῦ ἐνεργείᾳ καὶ ἀγαθότητι· 4.10 τὰ μὲν ἀμείνω τὴν γνώμην ἐπὶ τελειότερον ἄγων σκοπόν, τὰ δὲ χείρω καὶ πλημμελῶς ἀναστρεφόμενα οὐκ ἀποστερῶν τῆς ἑαυτοῦ βασιλικῆς καὶ ὁμονοητικῆς καὶ ἀμερίστου προστασίας, ἀλλ' ἐν ἐφέσει καθιστῶν αὐτὰ καὶ συννοίᾳ τῆς χορηγοῦ τῶν ὁλικῶν ἀγαθῶν ὁμοουσίου τριάδος· καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς καλλιεργοῦσι συλλαμβανόμενος, μετὰ τοῦ πάντων ἐξῃρημένος εἶναι οὕτως, ὅτι ἄλλῳ μὲν τῶν ἀποστόλων διάγοντι ἐν Ἰνδίᾳ, ἑτέρῳ δ' ἐν Σπανίᾳ ἄλλῳ δ' ἐν ἄλλῳ τόπῳ ἕως τῆς ἐσχατιᾶς τῆς γῆς παρ' αὐτοῦ νενεμημένῳ τῆς ἑαυτοῦ ἀπλανοῦς καὶ ἀκιβδήλου μετεδίδου σοφίας· οὐ τῷδε μὲν νῦν, ἑτέρῳ δ' εἰςαῦθις παραγινόμενος, οὐδὲ τῷ μὲν μᾶλλον, τῷ δὲ ἔλαττον ἐπιπνέων, ἀλλ' ἅμα τε καὶ ἑκάστῳ ὁμοῦ καὶ διακεκριμένως ἀεὶ ὁμοίως ἐπιλάμπων, καθὰ καὶ ὁ εἰπὼν κύριος· «μεθ' ὑμῶν εἰμι πάσας τὰς ἡμέρας ἕως τῆς συντελείας τοῦ αἰ ῶνος.» 4.11 ἐπεὶ μή γε–ἐπειδὴ αὐτοὶ τὴν παρ' Ἰωάννῃ 50 κειμένην θεολογίαν περὶ τοῦ πνεύματος ἔνθα εἶπεν· «πνεῦμα ὁ θεός» μεταφέρουσιν εἰς τὸν θεὸν καὶ πατέρα, λέγοντες διὰ τὸ εἶναι πνεῦμα αὐτὸν οὕτω γεγράφθαι, ἔτι δὲ ἐπειδὴ γέγραπται καί· «πνεῦμα τοῦ προσώπου ἡμῶν Χριστὸς κύριος·» – ἆρα καὶ τὸν παρέρα καὶ τὸν υἱὸν ἅτε πνεῦμα τοῖς ἄλλοις συναριθμήσουσι λειτουργικοῖς πνεύμασιν; εἰ δὲ τοῦτο οὐχ οὕτως, οὐδὲ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα νοεῖται μετὰ τῶν ἄλλων πνευμάτων. ἀρχάγγελος γὰρ οὔκ ἐστιν. ὁ γὰρ Μιχαὴλ καὶ Γαβριὴλ καὶ οἱ κατ' αὐτούς εἰσιν ἀρχάγγελοι· μετ' ἐκείνους δὲ οὐδὲ αἱρετικοὶ εἴποιεν ἂν τετάχθαι τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα τοῦ θεοῦ. 4.12 ποῦ οὖν λοιπὸν ἢ μετὰ ποίων κτισμάτων τάσσεσθαι δοκιμάζουσιν αὐτό; μετὰ γὰρ τὸν θεὸν φύσιν ἄλλην λογικὴν ἀπὸ γραφῶν οὐκ ἐδιδάχθημεν ἢ τῶν πολλῶν πνευμάτων καὶ καθ' ἡμᾶς σωμάτων. 4.13 ἔτι σοφιστικῶς ἐκ τῶν προκειμένων ἐπάγουσιν· ὁ πατὴρ καὶ ὁ υἱὸς «ἀληθινός», τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα «ἀλήθεια» γέγραπται, ὡς ἀπᾴδοντος τούτου. ἔστιν δὲ ταὐτόν, καθὰ ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ δέδεικται λόγῳ, καὶ οὐ διαφέρει τοῦτο ἐκείνου. 5.ν Περὶ τῶν λεγόντων, ὅτι «μονογενοῦς ὄντος τοῦ θεοῦ λόγου, τί τὸ πνεῦμα καλέσομεν;» καὶ περὶ τοῦ μαρτυρεῖσθαι τὸν υἱὸν μονογενῆ. τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα ἓν καὶ μόνον· καὶ πάλιν τὸν υἱὸν λόγον· τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα, ῥῆμα. καὶ περὶ συγκρίσεως· καὶ περὶ τοῦ μὴ εἶναι παράδειγμα τοῦ ἀσυγκρίτου οὐσίας. 5.1 Πρὸς ταῦτα οἱ ποικιλώτατοι καὶ πολυτροπώτατοι κατὰ τὸν λόγον οὐκ οἶδα, εἰ μὴ καὶ κατὰ τὴν γνώμην, πάντως δὲ ὅτι καὶ τοῦτο οἱ τῆς ἁπλουστέρας καὶ ἀληθεστέρας διδασκαλίας ἀλλότριοι αἱρετικοὶ ἀναστρέφοντες πολλάκις τὰ αὐτὰ ῥήματα, φασίν· «μονογενὴς ἐκλήθη ὁ θεὸς λόγος, ἐπειδὴ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα οὐκ ἐκ τῆς ὑποστάσεώς ἐστιν τοῦ πατρός. ἐπεὶ εἰ αὐτὸς μὲν οὐκ ἂν ἐλέχθη μονογενής, τὸ δὲ
pass_a_gloss: [Continuing: For Gabriel, speaking to Daniel, or announcing good news to the God-bearing] virgin, was not also in heaven in substance, as in thought, but at that time spent time on earth only. Nor are they uncontained by the ages; for 'he who makes', it says, 'his angels spirits, and his ministers a flaming fire'. 4.7 They do not do a single one of the things that come about from the Holy Spirit, but they even serve him, as the archangel Gabriel showed, having ministered to the God-bearer Mary and having said: 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you'. Neither, then, is man their temple, as he is of God and of his Spirit and of the only-begotten Son. They are not included together with God. Not one single angelic hypostasis is there, but one even hard to number. 4.8 But the Holy Spirit, shining beyond all, came forth naturally united and of one form, timelessly, from the unspeakable and beyond being and before being and universal and formless paternal hypostasis, and has been called divine; and he is one, unmultiplied, good, ungrudging, unapproachable, not circumscribed by all thinkings, of infinite power, unfailing [the copy-text reads 'unchosen'], existing uniquely; and by nature both holy and Spirit of God, and being nothing of all things, but God, being both in heaven and with us, cause for all of all good things; present to the wholes immaterially, without form, without change of shape; 4.9 and not standing away from being seated together unspeakably with the Father, and spreading out everywhere and making room, and dwelling in all things unmixed; and stepping into the thoughts both of us and of those unseen by us, and examining all things exactly, although knowing all things; and sounding within without voice, and hearing souls crying from within in silence, and pitying all of them in all things without delay, and strengthening, and giving unspeakable gladness to the natures in every place; encompassing the standing together of this universe, and having all things under himself; and enlightening with divine light and doing good by his immense working and goodness; 4.10 leading the things better in will to a more perfect aim, and the things worse and living out of tune not depriving of his own kingly and concord-making and undivided protection, but setting them in longing and reflection of the consubstantial Trinity, the supplier of the universal goods; and helping together all who work at the good, along with being set apart above all, so that to one of the apostles staying in India, to another in Spain, to another in another place as far as the edge of the earth, allotted by him, he imparted his own unwandering and unadulterated wisdom; not coming to this one now and to another hereafter, nor breathing upon one more and another less, but at once and upon each, together and distinctly, always alike shining upon them, just as also the Lord who said: 'I am with you all the days until the completion of the age'. 4.11 Since surely not [the sentence breaks off] — since they themselves carry over the theology about the Spirit lying in John, where he said: 'God is Spirit', to God and Father, saying that it was written so because he is spirit, and further since it is also written: 'Spirit of our face, Christ the Lord' — will they then also number together the Father and the Son, as spirit, with the other serving spirits? But if this is not so, neither is the Holy Spirit thought of with the other spirits. For he is not an archangel. For Michael and Gabriel and those like them are archangels; and not even heretics would say that the Holy Spirit of God has been ranked after those. 4.12 Where then, for the rest, or with what sort of creatures do they judge it right to rank him? For after God we were not taught from Scriptures another rational nature than that of the many spirits and of bodies like ours. 4.13 Further, sophistically, from the things set out they bring on: the Father and the Son are written 'true', but the Spirit 'truth', as though this is out of tune. But it is the same, as was shown in the first book, and this does not differ from that. 5.ν [Chapter title:] About those who say: 'Since God the Word is only-begotten, what shall we call the Spirit?' And about the Son being attested as only-begotten. The Holy Spirit one and only; and again the Son, Word; the Holy Spirit, utterance. And about comparison; and about there being no example of the incomparable substance. 5.1 To these things the most intricate and most many-turning in speech, I do not know whether also in mind, but certainly in this too, the heretics who are strangers to the simpler and truer teaching, turning over many times the same words, say: 'God the Word was called only-begotten because the Holy Spirit is not from the hypostasis of the Father. pass_b_english: … virgin (Luke 1:26-27), he was not in heaven as well in his substance, as he was in thought, but was at that time on earth only. Nor are the angels beyond the bounds of the ages; for “he who makes,” it says, “his angels spirits, and his ministers a flaming fire” (Psalm 104:4).

They do not do a single one of the things done by the Holy Spirit; rather, they serve him, as the archangel Gabriel showed when he ministered to Mary, the Mother of God, and said, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you” (Luke 1:35). Nor, then, is man their temple, as he is the temple of God and of his Spirit and of the only-begotten Son. They are not counted together with God. And the angelic hypostasis is not some single one; the angels are past numbering.

But the Holy Spirit, radiant beyond all things, came forth timelessly, of one nature and one form with it, from the ineffable, super-essential, pre-essential, universal and formless hypostasis of the Father, and he has been named divine. He is one, not multiplied, good, without envy, inaccessible, not to be circumscribed by any thought, infinite in power, unfailing, existing in a way that is his alone. He is by nature holy and the Spirit of God; he is none of the things that exist, but God, who is both in heaven and with us, the cause for all of every good thing. He is present to the whole universe without matter, without form, without change of shape.

Yet he does not depart from his ineffable seat beside the Father. He spreads out everywhere and pervades all, and dwells in all things without being mingled with them. He enters into the thoughts both of us and of those who are invisible to us, and searches all things exactly, though he knows all things (1 Corinthians 2:10). Without a voice he sounds within; he hears souls crying out within in silence, and takes pity on them all in all things without delay, and strengthens them, and gives unspeakable gladness to every nature everywhere. He holds together the frame of this universe and has all things under himself. He enlightens with divine light, and does good by his boundless working and goodness.

Those of better will he leads toward a more perfect goal. Those that are worse, and live amiss, he does not deprive of his kingly protection, which makes for concord and is undivided; instead he sets them longing for, and pondering, the consubstantial Trinity, which supplies every good thing in the universe. He works together with all who labour at what is good, while being set apart above all. So it was that to one of the apostles staying in India, to another in Spain, and to others in other places to the end of the earth, each apportioned his place by him, he imparted his own unerring and unadulterated wisdom. He did not come to this one now and to another later, nor breathe more on one and less on another, but shone upon all at once and upon each, together and distinctly, always alike, just as the Lord, too, said: “I am with you all the days until the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

For surely not — since they themselves transfer to God and Father the theology about the Spirit that stands in John, where he said, “God is Spirit” (John 4:24), saying that it was written so because he is spirit; and further, since it is also written, “The Spirit of our face, Christ the Lord” (Lamentations 4:20 LXX) — will they then number the Father and the Son too, as spirit, with the other ministering spirits? But if this is not so, neither is the Holy Spirit to be thought of with the other spirits. For he is not an archangel. Michael and Gabriel and those like them are archangels; and not even heretics would say that the Holy Spirit of God has been ranked after them.

Where, then, or among what kind of creatures do they think fit to rank him after all? For after God we have been taught from the Scriptures of no other rational nature than that of the many spirits and of bodies such as ours.

Further, they draw a sophistical conclusion from the passages set out above: the Father and the Son are written “true”, but the Spirit “truth”, as if this were out of tune with that. But it is the same, as was shown in the first book, and this does not differ from that.

Against those who say, “Since God the Word is only-begotten, what shall we call the Spirit?” On the Son being attested as only-begotten. The Holy Spirit is one and only; and again, the Son is the Word, the Holy Spirit is the utterance. On comparison; and that there is no example of the incomparable substance.

lemmas.gloss: of one nature with, naturally united

choices.issue: Paragraphs dropped; the section was about 64% of the expected length
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English opened with the fragment 'by essence, as by thought', then dropped the rest of 4.6 (the angels bounded by time; Psalm 104:4), all of 4.7 (the angels serve the Spirit; Gabriel and Luke 1:35; man not their temple; angels past numbering), all of 4.8 and 4.9 (the Spirit's timeless procession, his attributes, his presence everywhere) and the first half of 4.10, resuming mid-sentence at 'And to him in Spain'. It also read 'nor of the many spirits' for 'than that of the many spirits' (4.12), 'the first argument' for the first book (4.13), and 'the Holy Spirit, the Word' where the 5.ν title sets Word (the Son) against utterance (the Spirit). '(Matt 28:20)' written in full; Lamentations 4:20 marked LXX; 'Wherefore', '[us]' and '[to us]' removed.

choices.why: The section opens mid-sentence; 'when Gabriel spoke with Daniel, or brought the good news to the Mother of God' ends the previous section.

choices.english: Nor are the angels beyond the bounds of the ages
choices.why: The angels were made (Psalm 104:4) and so are contained within time; 'the angels' named for clarity.
The copy-text's ἀνέκλεκτον ('not chosen') makes no sense among the divine attributes; read as ἀνέκλειπτον ('unfailing'), a one-letter slip. See problems.
Plural 'the wholes' is the usual Greek for the universe.

choices.english: searches all things exactly, though he knows all things (1 Corinthians 2:10)
choices.why: Clear echo of 'the Spirit searches all things'; Didymus adds that the searching is not for want of knowledge.

choices.english: takes pity on them all in all things
choices.why: Feminine πάσας refers back to the souls.

choices.term: ἄλλῳ μὲν … ἐν Ἰνδίᾳ, ἑτέρῳ δ' ἐν Σπανίᾳ
choices.english: to one of the apostles staying in India, to another in Spain
choices.why: Didymus does not name them (Thomas and Paul by tradition); no names added.
The copy-text breaks off with a dash and restarts the sentence; the anacoluthon is kept.

choices.term: τὴν … θεολογίαν περὶ τοῦ πνεύματος … «πνεῦμα ὁ θεός»
choices.english: the theology about the Spirit … “God is Spirit”
choices.why: Didymus reads John 4:24 as a statement of the Holy Spirit's Godhead which the heretics apply to the Father; 'Spirit' capitalised to keep his reading visible.
Misprint in the copy-text for τὸν πατέρα.
λόγος here is a book of the treatise (Book 1 of On the Trinity), not an argument.

choices.english: Against those who say … On comparison; and that there is no example of the incomparable substance.
choices.why: Set as its own paragraph; λόγος (Word, the Son) and ῥῆμα (utterance, the Spirit) kept distinct.
The section ends mid-sentence; the rest of the heretics' argument opens the next section.
50 is a printed page number, page debris; αἰ ῶνος is a line-break split.
